courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: Tagged pointers: a version counter beside the pointer
md: Tagged pointer = pointer plus a counter compared and swapped as one unit, bumped on every successful CAS. It turns "same value" into "same value and same version".

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Per-query deltas, paired tests and confidence intervals
md: Queries are not the only noise source. If a stage is trained, its score also varies with the random seed. Use the same seeds and checkpoints for every stage you are not ablating, and when the ablated stage itself is retrained, run several seeds and report the spread, or a seed-to-seed swing can masquerade as a component effect.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Sequential vs random ids, and why random ids are not authorization
md: Parler's public posts were meant to be readable one at a time. Sequential ids plus no rate limit turned "anyone can read a post" into "anyone can copy the entire site, with GPS locations". Authorization decides who may read an object; rate limits and unpredictable ids decide how cheaply someone can read all of them. You need both.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: What Active Directory is: one directory for thousands of machines
md: A domain is not a wall. Domains in one forest trust each other automatically, and the Enterprise Admins group of the forest root is an administrator in every domain (next lesson). Plan protection for the whole forest, not one domain at a time.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: AS-REP roasting and password spraying against AD
md: Turning off pre-authentication hands out crackable material to anyone; 4768 with pre-auth type 0 finds it. Spraying hides under per-account lockout; count distinct accounts per source in 4771 and 4776, not failures per account.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Tiered administration, Protected Users and LAPS
md: Tiering fails quietly through agents. A backup, monitoring or patching tool that runs as SYSTEM on DCs, managed from a Tier 1 console, makes that console Tier 0. List everything installed on DCs and everyone who controls it.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Format string bugs as read and write primitives
md: A format string bug is a primitive factory: the read directives leak, and %n writes. The cure is structural and cheap: constant format strings, enforced by -Werror=format-security and static analysis.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: Reading a leaderboard: harness, noise, cost and contamination
md: Checklist for any agent leaderboard number: which subset and version; which harness, tools, step and cost budget; one attempt or best of many (pass@k vs pass^1 vs pass^k); how many tasks and trials, with an interval; and whether the tasks predate the model's training cutoff.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Why an agent cannot just replay its whole history
md: A memory system is defined by four decisions: what to write, how to reconcile it with what is already stored, what to retrieve for a given step, and what to forget. Retrieval alone is RAG; the write and forget decisions are what make it memory.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: Best-of-N with an imperfect verifier: the accuracy ceiling
md: FPR sets the ceiling, TPR sets the speed. With enough samples, best-of-N accuracy converges to the verifier's precision $pt / (pt + (1-p)f)$. Raising TPR only means you need fewer samples to get there.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Prompt injection: when data becomes instructions
md: Treat every token the model reads as a possible instruction from whoever wrote it. You cannot reliably make the model ignore it, so limit what obeying it can achieve.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: System prompt leakage and sensitive information disclosure
md: Assume the system prompt will be read by users and attackers. Put nothing in it that would hurt if published, and enforce every rule that matters in code.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: A crystal as data: lattice, fractional coordinates, periodicity
md: A crystal is a set of atom types, fractional coordinates in [0, 1), and a 3x3 lattice. Cartesian position is $f$ times $L$, coordinates wrap mod 1, and every distance must use the minimum image.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Detection is a z-test on the green count
md: A tiny false positive rate is not zero at scale. $z > 4$ means a one-sided p of $3.2 \times 10^{-5}$: scan a million human documents and expect about 32 false flags. Hugging Face's `WatermarkDetector` defaults to $z > 3$, where the rate is $1.3 \times 10^{-3}$. Pick the threshold for the cost of a false accusation.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Why the mean and standard deviation hide outliers
md: Masking is the main failure of mean-based scores: several outliers inflate the standard deviation and hide one another. The NIST handbook also warns that applying a single-outlier test repeatedly does not fix this, because the first test may already report nothing.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Evaluating detectors when 1 percent of points are anomalies
md: Do not report accuracy for anomaly detection: labeling everything normal scores 99 percent accuracy here. Be wary of ROC-AUC alone too. Report AP or a PR curve, plus precision@k at the review budget you actually have.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: OAuth 2.0: delegated access without sharing a password
md: Misconception: "Sign in with X" means OAuth logged you in. Plain OAuth only says some client got a token. Building login on raw access tokens has caused real impersonation bugs; OpenID Connect adds the missing pieces.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Validating a JWT correctly: algorithm, signature, iss, aud, exp, nbf
md: Validation is a fixed checklist the receiver owns: pinned algorithm, trusted issuer's key, signature, iss, aud, exp and nbf with small leeway, type. A library helps only when you pass it every one of those rules.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Three maps of a secure SDLC: Microsoft SDL, OWASP SAMM, NIST SSDF
md: SDL says what one company does, SAMM measures how mature you are, and SSDF is the reference list that governments and customers ask you to attest to. Most programmes use SAMM to plan and SSDF to report. You will also meet BSIMM (Building Security In Maturity Model), which describes what real companies' programmes do rather than prescribing a target.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Secrets scanning and pre-commit hooks
md: Rewriting git history to remove a secret does not un-leak it. Forks, clones, CI caches and anyone who fetched in the meantime still have it. Treat any committed secret as compromised: rotate it, then look at the provider's logs for its use.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Programme decisions: secure defaults, memory safety, Secure by Design
md: Finding bugs is linear work; removing bug classes compounds. A mature programme spends part of its budget on defaults, paved roads and language choices that make the next thousand findings never happen.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Why a question is not a short version of its answer
md: Search is asymmetric. Queries and documents differ in length, form and role, and relevance means *answers*, not *looks like*. Tell the model which side each text is on.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Retries that do not stampede: backoff, jitter and Retry-After
md: Retry with: honor Retry-After when present (plus a little randomness); otherwise capped exponential backoff with full jitter; a maximum number of attempts and a total time budget; and retries only for retryable errors (429, 5xx, timeouts), never for 400-class mistakes (4xx codes such as 400 Bad Request mean the request itself is wrong, so it fails the same way again), billing or quota errors.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Why counter++ from two threads loses updates
md: The bug is the gap between the read and the write. Any fix must make the whole read-modify-write indivisible, either with a lock around it or with an atomic operation.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: Sigmoid outputs and pooling patch scores into a clip score
md: Do not apply softmax across AudioSet classes and then threshold. A clip with dog and speech would have to split probability between them. Use the model's per-class sigmoid scores, and tune a threshold per class if you need hard yes/no tags.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Password rules that work: NIST SP 800-63B
md: Forced periodic rotation makes passwords weaker, not stronger: people make the smallest possible change. CISA's advisory on Scattered Spider (a cybercriminal group that targets companies through their IT help desks, lesson 12) repeats NIST's advice to refrain from recurring password changes. Change on evidence of compromise instead.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: SSO at a glance, detection signals, and responding to takeover
md: Identity attacks leave traces in authentication logs: failures, travel, new devices, MFA changes. Centralising login through SSO makes those traces easy to collect, and makes the IdP the account to protect most.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: One API in front of many models: the Converse call
md: `inferenceConfig` has only four fields. Putting a model-specific parameter there is a mistake; it belongs in `additionalModelRequestFields`, and it only works for models that define it.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Training from scratch: latent weights and the STE
md: Training a BitNet is not cheaper than training an FP16 model with today's code. Latent weights, gradients and optimizer states are high precision, and the FAQ notes their training ran in FP16/BF16 with no speedup. The savings are at inference.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Branchless code: cmov, masks and lookup tables
md: Branchless code trades a *possible* misprediction for *always* doing the work of both sides plus the select. Always check the compiler output (Compiler Explorer, the godbolt.org website that shows the assembly a compiler produces, or the `-S` flag, which makes the compiler write assembly instead of an object file) before hand-rewriting: the optimizer may already have done it, or may have a good reason not to.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Choosing an engine: tradeoffs, write stalls and failure modes
md: Misconception: "LSM-trees have no write amplification because they only write sequentially." They write sequentially, but every byte is rewritten as it moves down levels: about 33x in RocksDB's leveled example. The win is in I/O pattern and batching, not in writing less, and on some workloads a B+tree writes fewer bytes.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Why drop the tokenizer, and why raw bytes are expensive
md: Bytes remove the vocabulary and its blind spots, but multiply the number of positions by roughly 4. Since compute is about $2mT$, a byte model is only practical if the big network runs on far fewer positions than there are bytes.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: The same bugs in Rust: compile errors, panics, and what slips through
md: Misconception: "Rust has no runtime checks, everything is proven at compile time." Lifetimes and aliasing are checked at compile time; indexing, `RefCell` borrows and debug-mode overflow are checked at run time. The design goal is that every remaining failure is defined, not that there are none.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Cache lines: the cache moves 64 bytes, never just one
md: Arrange data so that what you use together sits together, and walk it in address order. Stride 1 is the cheapest pattern there is.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Pruning by influence and grouping supernodes
md: Influence is unsigned. A feature that strongly *inhibits* the answer scores as high as one that promotes it. Use influence to decide what to look at, then read the signed edges to decide what it does.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Estimating propensities: swaps, EM, harvesting, dual learning
md: EM can only separate rank from document if the same documents appear at different ranks, and those overlaps must link all ranks together. When ranker 2 was D, E, B, A, C instead, ranks {1, 4} and {2, 3, 5} never shared a document, the relative scale between the two groups was unidentifiable, and EM's answer for rank 2 depended on its starting point: 0.63 starting from 0.5, 0.53 starting from 0.3 (truth 0.5).

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Stopping CSRF: SameSite, tokens, Origin and Fetch Metadata
md: Cross-site scripting defeats every CSRF defence, as the Samy worm showed by reading MySpace's token. CSRF defences assume the attacker is outside your origin. Fix XSS first; then CSRF defences mean something.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: The cloud from a security view: computers you rent through an API
md: In the cloud every resource is managed through a public API, so whoever holds valid credentials can act from anywhere. The main walls are identities, permissions and configuration, not the office network.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Secrets and keys: KMS, envelope encryption and secret stores
md: Encryption at rest only protects you from people who cannot use the key. If the same over-broad role can both read the bucket and call Decrypt, as an application role often can, the encryption adds an audit trail but no barrier. Grant `kms:Decrypt` as narrowly as the data itself.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Evaluating a clustering with and without labels
md: Look at the first two bars. The k = 2 clustering with the *better* inertia, 28.8333, scores ARI 0.4109, while the local optimum with the worse inertia, 30.4167, scores 0.7734. Optimising the objective harder moved the answer away from the truth. Inertia is a proxy, and this is what it means for a proxy to be imperfect: never argue from inertia to correctness.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: What -O0, -O2 and -O3 actually switch on
md: An -O level is a bundle of passes. -O0 keeps every variable in memory for debuggability; -O2 is the standard speed level; -O3, -Os, -Og and -Ofast each trade something (size, speed, debuggability, strictness) for something else.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: PGO, -march=native and -ffast-math: speed with strings attached
md: PGO, -march and fast-math can each beat any -O level, but each adds a condition: representative profiles, a known target CPU, and numerics that tolerate reordering.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Why a concurrent test can pass a million times and still be wrong
md: A concurrent test that passes tells you only that the schedules your machine happened to pick were fine. To learn anything about the others you must either enumerate schedules (loom) or check the ordering rules on the schedule you got (TSan).

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: Self-consistency: every point on a trajectory maps to its origin
md: A consistency model is not a one-step denoiser. A network trained with plain squared-error regression (the L2 loss) to $x_0$ from $x_T$ learns the conditional mean, which is blurry for images and collapses in the toy. The consistency function is a deterministic map along ODE trajectories, so its outputs keep the full data spread.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Why hash mod N reshuffles almost every key
md: A central lookup table (key range to server) also gives minimal movement, and many databases use one. The catch is that every client must fetch and agree on the table. Consistent hashing lets each client compute the owner from the key and the server list alone.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Too few results: relaxation ladders and post-hoc constraints
md: Three layers, three tools: per-document requirements are **filters**, per-document preferences are a **weighted score**, and requirements on the list as a whole are a **re-ranking pass**. When filters starve the list, relax in a declared order, keep the non-negotiables hard, and say what you relaxed.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: One kernel, many tenants: the container threat model
md: Misconception: "root in a container is harmless because it is only container root". Without user namespaces, UID 0 inside the container is UID 0 on the host, held back only by dropped capabilities, seccomp and the LSM. Remove those fences, or find a bug in them, and it is real root.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: A hardened pod spec, line by line
md: Hardened default for application pods: no token, non-root, RuntimeDefault seccomp, no privilege escalation, read-only root filesystem, drop ALL capabilities, explicit writable volumes, resource limits, image by digest.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Network policies: from default allow to default deny
md: Misconception: "the database is internal, so it is not exposed". Internal means reachable by every pod in the cluster unless a policy says otherwise. Treat the pod network as a hostile network.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a hardening map and where to practise
md: Legal line: everything in this course is for clusters you own or have written permission to test. Scanning the internet for open kubelets or Docker APIs, or using one you find, is unauthorised access under laws such as the US CFAA and the UK Computer Misuse Act, whatever the intent.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: A five-turn session: diffs, state and generated queries
md: Let the LLM decide **what changed**; let code decide **what the state is** and **what the query is**. This split makes carryover free, makes every change visible in logs, and turns the hardest part into a small, testable classification problem.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Poking the chain: truncate it, break it, reword it
md: Each test rules out one failure class, nothing more. A CoT that passes truncation and mistake tests is causally used, but it can still omit a factor (as in Turpin's hints). Lanham et al. call this a defense-in-depth approach: no single test certifies faithfulness.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Why a reranker reads the query and the document together
md: A bi-encoder pays the document cost once, offline. A cross-encoder pays the full transformer cost for every (query, document) pair at query time. That single fact explains both why it is more accurate and why it can only rerank a shortlist.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: What cryptography promises, and to whom
md: Misconception: "nobody knows our format, so it is safe". That is security through obscurity. Formats leak, binaries get reverse-engineered, employees leave. If learning the algorithm breaks your system, it was never secure.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Password hashing and key derivation: slow on purpose
md: Do not use one key for two jobs (say, encryption and MAC, or client-to-server and server-to-client). Derive separate keys with HKDF and distinct labels.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Layout algebra: composition, tiling and partitioning
md: Composition reshapes, divide tiles, slicing selects. local_tile picks a CTA's tile, local_partition or a TV layout picks a thread's share, and both are just layout algebra applied to the same tensor.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: CXL protocols, device types and the path of one load
md: Pooling and sharing are different. In **pooling** each slice of memory belongs to exactly one host at a time; it just moves between hosts. In **sharing** (CXL 3.0) several hosts map the same bytes at once and hardware keeps them coherent. Most CXL disaggregation designs, including Pond, use pooling.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Why a loop over objects wastes most of each cache line
md: SoA is not automatically faster. Its advantage is exactly the fraction of each record that a loop does *not* touch. A loop that uses every field gains nothing from the layout change, and some access patterns get worse (lesson 2).

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Seeds and RNG state: a different problem from kernels
md: A fixed seed proves nothing about kernel determinism, and batch-invariant kernels prove nothing about the sampler. Run two separate experiments: hold the batch fixed and vary the seed to test sampling, and hold the seed fixed while varying batch size and position to test the kernels. A test that varies both at once cannot attribute a failure.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Threat-modelling a pipeline: poisoned pipeline execution
md: Protecting the workflow file is not enough. With I-PPE the attacker never touches it: they edit what it calls. Treat everything the privileged job executes (Makefiles, scripts, test files, tool configs, lockfiles) as part of the pipeline.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: The forward process: masking as noise, and its exact reverse
md: The forward process is fixed and trivial. The only thing to learn is a **mask predictor**: given a partly masked sequence, output a distribution over the vocabulary at every masked position. It needs no timestep input.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Goodput: requests per GPU that meet both SLOs
md: Goodput = the highest rate at which at least 90% (or your target) of requests meet every latency SLO, divided by the GPUs used. It is the number disaggregation is designed to raise.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: CAGRA search on the GPU, and picking an index
md: Choosing: **DiskANN** when the data is far larger than RAM and an SSD is acceptable (a few ms per query at high recall on one machine). **CAGRA** when vectors fit in GPU memory and you need high throughput or fast builds; IVF-PQ initial graph builds can run in batches on datasets larger than GPU memory. **CAGRA then HNSW** when you build on GPUs but serve on CPUs.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Failure modes, fixes, and DPO in production recipes
md: Choosing among the variants: DPO is the default for paired data with an SFT model. Use IPO-style or early-stopped training when labels are near-deterministic and you need to stay close to the reference; KTO when feedback is unpaired or imbalanced; ORPO or SimPO when a reference model is too costly. Whatever you choose, keep the chosen likelihood and output length under watch.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Flipping writes, cutting over and deleting the old path
md: Common failure modes: a write path nobody knew about keeps writing only the old store (find it with loud errors and comparisons); deletes resurrected by the backfill; reads switched before the completeness job is rerun; and deleting old data before every reader of the old field is gone.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: The three budgets a model must fit on a small device
md: A model fits a device only if three numbers fit: bytes of weights versus flash, peak bytes of live activations versus RAM, and cycles per inference versus the latency target. Check all three before training anything.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: L1: putting the token budget in the prompt
md: L1-Exact spends the requested budget even when the problem is easy, because its reward penalizes being too short. When the goal is a worst-case cost cap rather than an exact length, use the Max formulation, which matched or beat L1-Exact while often using up to 2x fewer tokens.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Combinatorial optimisation and factorial HMMs
md: Do not read CO's perfect toy score as "CO beats event detection". CO was given the exact appliance powers and only three appliances with no sum collisions. Add one appliance whose power equals a sum of others, or real-world power that drifts, and per-sample matching breaks while temporal models degrade more gracefully.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: From pairwise links to entities: clustering
md: Watch cluster sizes. One low-threshold edge between two big clusters creates a giant cluster that silently merges thousands of records. Alert on clusters that grow suddenly, and require stronger evidence for edges that would join two large clusters.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Event loops in practice: libuv, timers, thread pools
md: An event loop scales because idle connections cost only a kernel watch and a small struct, and readiness is pushed to a ready list instead of scanned. It stays fast only if every callback is short: push disk I/O, DNS and CPU-heavy work to a pool, and split long jobs into chunks.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Contamination: when test queries leak into training data
md: A public benchmark score for a model trained on web-scale data is an upper bound on its skill on your queries, not an estimate. Before trusting a gain, ask whether the model, the synthetic training data or the judge (a language model that grades relevance in place of human labelers) could have seen these queries.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Sandboxing as a layer: how Android hardened after Stagefright
md: A sandbox does not make a bug less exploitable; it makes successful exploitation worth less, and forces the attacker to find and chain another bug. Put the riskiest code (parsers of untrusted input) in the least privileged process.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: The setting: data that is not allowed to leave the device
md: The defining property is not cryptography. It is that **the data stays put and only parameters move**. In the standard description of the setting, a central orchestration server organizes the training but never sees raw data.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: ACORN-gamma: expand every neighbor list by gamma
md: Misconception: "just raise M in HNSW". The paper notes that Qdrant's earlier densification idea did this, but $M$ also sets HNSW's level multiplier $m_L = 1/\ln M$, so raising it flattens the hierarchy, and HNSW is sensitive to its number of levels. ACORN keeps $M$ (and therefore $m_L$ and the level structure) fixed and expands the lists by $\gamma$ instead.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: Online softmax: exact attention one block at a time
md: Online softmax is exact. The running max is only for numerical safety (keeping $e^x$ from overflowing); any consistent reference point gives the same $O/l$. Every FlashAttention version computes the same math; they differ only in how the work is mapped onto the hardware.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: The training target: straight lines and their velocity
md: The training loss does not go to zero even for a perfect network. Different pairs pass through the same $(x_t, t)$ with different targets, and a regression can only output their average. That average is the field you want, as lesson 3 shows.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: What 8 and 4 bits can hold: E4M3, E5M2 and E2M1
md: Exponent bits buy **range**, mantissa bits buy **precision**. E4M3 rounds with at most 6.25% relative error but spans only about 18 binades; E5M2 spans about 32 binades at 12.5%; E2M1 (FP4) spans 3.58 binades at up to 25%.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Why write() returning does not mean your data is safe
md: Durable means: the bytes reached stable media **and** everything needed to find them (file size, block map, directory entry) did too. `write()` gives you neither; `fsync()` on the file and its directory gives you both.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Writing good harnesses: fast, deterministic and structure-aware
md: A harness that crashes on its own (a null pointer it should have checked, an `abort()` on documented bad input) floods you with false reports. Treat harness bugs as bugs: the fuzzer is only as trustworthy as the target function.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Symbolic and concolic execution: solving for the input
md: Symbolic execution is not magic search. It struggles with floating point, cryptographic hashes (a solver cannot invert SHA-256), huge loops and code it cannot see, such as system calls. Use it on the narrow, hard checks a fuzzer cannot pass, not as a replacement for fuzzing.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Transpositions and Indel: which edits count changes the answer
md: Two libraries that both say "Damerau-Levenshtein" can disagree, and "ratio" in RapidFuzz is Indel based, not Levenshtein based. When a threshold copied from one tool behaves oddly in another, check which distance and which normalization each uses.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: The Astrometry.net quad code, computed step by step
md: Quad code = coordinates of C and D in the frame where A is (0,0) and B is (1,1). Four numbers, independent of where the quad is, how it is turned, or how big it looks.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Better cells on the sphere: S2 cubes and H3 hexagons
md: H3 parent containment is only approximate. Seven hexagons cannot exactly tile a larger hexagon, so a child cell's area can stick out of its parent's boundary. The index hierarchy is exact logically (truncating an ID always gives the same parent), so aggregating by parent ID is consistent, but do not treat a parent's polygon as the exact union of its children.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Rounding, the small and large pools, and segment sizes
md: Every request is rounded to 512 bytes, routed by size (at most 1 MiB small, otherwise large), and served from a block in that pool. Only a miss touches the driver, with a 2 MiB, 20 MiB or rounded-to-2-MiB segment.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: From registers to HBM: the GPU memory map
md: Speed and capacity trade off at every level: registers and shared memory are on the SM and fast but small, L2 is shared by all SMs, and HBM is large but far away. Kernel design is mostly about making each byte fetched from HBM count.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Timeline first: where the 14.52 ms actually goes
md: The GPU utilization that Nsight Systems reports is **time** utilization, not resource utilization. Its own guide says so: a single running memcpy counts as the same amount of utilization as a huge kernel that takes over all the cores, and concurrent operations in the same chunk can add up to more than 100 percent. A 100 percent busy GPU can still be doing almost nothing useful.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: One kernel, many threads: grids, blocks and SMs
md: Blocks must not depend on each other. A thread may not wait for, or read results produced by, a thread in a different block of the same grid, because that block may not have been scheduled yet. (Thread block clusters, in lesson 4, are the one opt-in exception.)

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Finding communities: modularity and the Leiden algorithm
md: Communities come from edge structure alone. Leiden never reads a description; it only sees nodes and weighted edges. That is why the extraction quality from lesson 2 decides the quality of the topics.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: RLVR: replacing the reward model with a program
md: RLVR changes where the reward comes from, not the RL algorithm. Tulu 3 ran RLVR with PPO; DeepSeek ran it with GRPO. The rest of this course is about GRPO, the algorithm that made RLVR cheap at scale.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: GTFS Realtime messages and decoding them in Python
md: With FULL_DATASET, each fetch is the entire current state. If a trip's update was in the last message but is missing from this one, the consumer must treat it as having no realtime data now, and the reference is explicit that no TripUpdate does **not** mean the trip is on time.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: What a side channel is: secrets leaking through how code runs
md: A side-channel attack does not break the mathematics. It breaks the assumption that an implementation reveals only its outputs. Every defence in this course makes some byproduct independent of the secret, hides the secret from the computation that leaks, or keeps the observer away.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: What 4 KiB pages cost a 16 GiB working set
md: Huge pages pay off three ways: one TLB entry covers 512 (or 262,144) times more memory, each miss walks fewer levels, and the page tables shrink. The kernel's THP doc calls the fourth effect, one page fault per 2 MiB instead of 512, almost irrelevant because it only happens on first touch.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Why a fixed-size state forgets and a KV cache does not
md: Pure SSMs are not simply worse. In the same NVIDIA study, Mamba-2 trained on 3.5T tokens beat the matching Transformer on average across standard zero-shot tasks. The gap is specific: copying, in-context learning and exact retrieval from the prompt.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Why a raw query is a poor probe for an unsupervised encoder
md: Short queries and long documents look different. A label-free encoder knows what *documents* resemble each other, but nobody taught it what *answers a question*. HyDE's trick is to stop comparing a question with answers at all.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Zones and conduits: the ISA/IEC 62443 way to segment
md: Zones are not VLANs. A VLAN (virtual LAN) is one way to separate traffic, but NIST lists VLANs as logical separation 'when physical separation may not be feasible'. A zone boundary needs an enforcement point, and a misconfigured switch trunk can quietly merge two zones.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Segmentation, DMZs, one-way gateways and allowlisting
md: A firewall rule that says 'allow 10.0.0.0/8 to OT, any port, temporary' is the most common way segmentation fails. Review the rule table regularly, expire temporary rules automatically, and alert on hits to rule 11: traffic nobody planned is either a misconfiguration or an intruder.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Differencing and picking a threshold with Otsu's method
md: Otsu always returns a threshold, even when nothing changed. On a pair with pure noise it will happily split the noise into two classes and flag a large fraction of the image. Check for a clear gap (or a minimum difference between class means) before trusting the mask.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Declaring, severity, the incident commander and the first hour
md: The IC decides and coordinates; they should not also be the person typing commands. When the IC is debugging, nobody is commanding.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Eradication and recovery: rebuild, credentials, krbtgt and backups
md: Replication is not backup. Synchronised copies (domain controllers, mirrored disks, cloud sync) receive the attacker's deletions and encryption as fast as your legitimate changes. Keep at least one copy offline and immutable, and practise restoring it.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Why escaping is fragile
md: Denylist filters ("block quotes, OR, UNION and --") are escaping's weaker cousin. They reject real input such as O'Brien, and they only stop the spellings someone thought of: SQL accepts comments, different case, different whitespace and many equivalent expressions. Lesson 9 shows a real product whose cleaning function was bypassed by finding a path where it was not applied.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Links, drains, timeouts and a CQ that never overflows
md: Size the **CQ** for the maximum number of completions that can be outstanding (including several per request for multishot operations, which post many completions from one request, lesson 5), not the SQ. Use `IORING_SETUP_CQSIZE` with `cq_entries`, and reap promptly.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Why a healthy cluster hides consistency bugs
md: Jepsen judges a system only by its history: what clients asked for and what they were told. A violation is reported only when **no** legal execution of the claimed model could explain that history, so a failure is a real bug, not a guess.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Search strategies and the trial budget
md: Match the strategy to the budget. Under about 20 trials, use a ranking (a heuristic, a cost model, or a curated list) and measure its top few. From tens to a few hundred, random sampling is a strong and honest baseline. Past a few hundred, evolutionary or local refinement pays off, and a learned model pays off at every budget.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The price of bypass, and when to choose something else
md: Two folk beliefs ixy tested and found weak: bigger rings do not add throughput (they add latency), and huge pages inside the driver itself changed throughput by only 1 to 3% at realistic ring sizes (5.5% at the largest). That test ran without the IOMMU. With the IOMMU on, ixy lost 62% of throughput on 4 KiB pages (the IOMMU's small TLB thrashes) and nothing on 2 MiB pages, so hugepages still matter a lot.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Why a teacher's soft targets beat one-hot labels
md: Training the student on the teacher's top-1 prediction alone (its single most likely class) (pseudo-labeling) is not the same thing. It keeps the teacher's decision but discards the relative probabilities of the other classes, which is exactly the extra signal that makes distillation work.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sharing keys and values across heads: MQA and GQA
md: GQA and MQA are architecture choices. They need training (or uptraining) and cannot be switched on at serving time, but they stack with every serving-time trick in the rest of this course.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Compressing long prompts (SnapKV, PyramidKV) and choosing a recipe
md: Choose by failure mode: FP8 for a near-free 2x; per-channel-key, per-token-value low-bit (KIVI, KVQuant) for 4x to 5x if kernels support it; eviction (StreamingLLM, H2O, SnapKV, PyramidKV) when context length is the problem and occasional lost tokens are acceptable.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Eviction and placement: what stays, what sinks, what is dropped
md: Do not evict a prefix's parent before its children. Because keys are chained, removing an early block makes every later block of that prefix unreachable, yet those stranded blocks still occupy space. SGLang's radix tree evicts leaves first for this reason, and Mooncake Store can evict a group of related objects (such as the separate K and V tensors of one entry) all or none.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Why one vector per document leaves accuracy behind
md: ColBERT is not a cross-encoder with a trick. Query tokens never attend to document tokens inside the transformer. All query-document interaction happens in MaxSim, which has no trainable parameters. That is exactly why document vectors can be stored in advance.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Why reasoning in word tokens is a bottleneck
md: Coconut's one change: in latent mode, the next input embedding is the previous position's last hidden state instead of the embedding of a sampled token.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: An index is a model: predicting where a key sits
md: A learned range index is a model of the key CDF plus two stored numbers per model, min_err and max_err. The model makes a guess; the error bounds turn the guess into a guarantee for every stored key.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: Why learn sparse vectors instead of dense ones
md: A learned sparse vector is still a bag of weighted terms, so it can live in a normal inverted index. The transformer only decides *which* terms get *how much* weight, including terms absent from the text.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: LambdaMART: boosted trees that fit the lambdas
md: LambdaMART = gradient boosted regression trees whose regression targets are the LambdaRank lambdas, recomputed after re-sorting at every round.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Where things live: the Linux filesystem from a defender's view
md: A detail worth remembering for later: if a program's file is deleted while it is still running, `/proc/<pid>/exe` shows the original path with ` (deleted)` appended (`proc_pid_exe(5)`). Legitimate software rarely does this; a process running from a deleted file in `/tmp` is a classic sign of an intruder cleaning up after starting a tool.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Packages and updates, and the xz-utils backdoor
md: Patching closes most known holes, so do it promptly and automatically where you can, and reboot when the kernel or core libraries change. Package signatures protect the path from repository to you; they cannot vouch for the people upstream.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Why relevance labels are the bottleneck of search evaluation
md: LLM-as-judge for relevance is a measurement instrument. Like any instrument, you calibrate it against a trusted reference (human gold labels) before you read numbers off it.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Pairwise preference, Elo and Bradley-Terry ratings
md: Do not rank by raw win percentage when models faced different opponents: beating weak models inflates it. BT accounts for who played whom. And never report a ranking without intervals; with few votes, neighbouring models are often statistically tied.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Continuous batching: scheduling every iteration
md: The scheduler's unit of work is a step with a token budget, not a request. Requests enter and leave between steps, and every step is a fresh decision about who gets how many tokens.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a prompt: rules, delimited inputs and the task
md: A good prompt separates three things the model must not confuse: the rules (stable), the input data (fenced in tags), and the task (stated plainly, ideally last). Then measure: every vendor guide says prompting is iterative and should be checked against test cases.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: From extracted strings to canonical IDs and a bool query
md: The `minimum_should_match` default depends on context. In Elasticsearch it is 1 only when the bool has `should` clauses and no `must` or `filter` clauses; otherwise it is 0, and the should clauses become optional score boosts. Put Berlin and remote as bare should clauses next to a filter list and *every* city passes.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Cutting decode: FIRST and single-token listwise ranking
md: Output tokens are the expensive kind for latency. Prefer designs whose answer is one token or one logit: pointwise labels, PRP in scoring mode, or FIRST-style first-token ranking.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Position bias, robustness and distilled rerankers
md: Pick the formulation by its failure mode: pointwise needs calibration, pairwise needs many calls, listwise needs a long context and a good initial order. Most practical gains come from controlling those failure modes (swapping, shuffling, cascades, distillation), not from a cleverer single prompt.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: Matching descriptors and Lowe's ratio test
md: Judge a match by how much better it is than the runner-up, not by its absolute distance. The ratio d1/d2 adapts to how distinctive each descriptor is.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The ABA problem: when a matching CAS is still wrong
md: CAS compares bits, not history. Any lock-free algorithm that frees or reuses nodes must either version its pointers or guarantee that no thread can still hold a reference to a node that gets reused.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: From templates to counts, time series and alerts
md: Parsing accuracy is not the goal; downstream behaviour is. SHISO parsed 93 percent of messages into the right groups and still produced 7 times the false alarms, because the templates it got wrong were ones the detector was sensitive to. Always evaluate a parser change by re-running the task that consumes its output.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Time: clocks, time zones and the order of events
md: Daylight saving time makes 'local time' worse: once a year, an hour of local timestamps happens twice. Two events at 01:30 local on that night cannot be ordered without the offset. Log in UTC.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Why models break past their trained length
md: RoPE is called a relative encoding, so it is tempting to think it should extrapolate for free. It does not: dimensions whose wavelength exceeds the training length never wrap, so in practice they leak absolute position, and new positions mean new, unseen angles.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Hiding communication, causal balance and Ulysses
md: Overlap condition: $c \ge F/B$. Fast links (NVLink, the TPU inter-chip interconnect or ICI) need blocks of about 1K tokens; slow links need tens of thousands. Causal masks require striping or zigzag chunk assignment, or the busiest rank sets the pace.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Spending compute at test time: more loops, early exits, shared caches
md: Per-token early exit saves FLOPs per token, but in batched serving tokens that exit early may sit idle waiting for others. Relaxed Recursive Transformers (Bae et al. 2024) propose **continuous depth-wise batching**, scheduling new work into slots freed by early exits; their simulation estimates 2 to 3x throughput, not a measured deployment.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: The wider PEFT family, and when LoRA falls short
md: Hu et al.'s footnote already warned that a small rank should not be expected to work for every task: if the target were a different language than pretraining, full fine-tuning (like LoRA with r equal to the model width) could win. Low intrinsic rank was measured on tasks that are close to what the model already knows.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Hidden, not gone: relearning, probing and quantization attacks
md: Low scores on forget benchmarks show suppressed outputs, not erased knowledge. Small fine-tunes, probes and even 4-bit quantization can bring "forgotten" knowledge back, because approximate unlearning moves the weights only slightly.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Disassemblers and decompilers: from bytes back to C
md: Reversing is a loop of hypotheses: name what you think a function does, check it against the assembly and against dynamic behaviour, and rename again. Stuxnet's analysts needed months and domain experts; your first samples will need hours. The method is the same.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Sharing intelligence and writing the analysis report
md: Write for the reader who must act. The executive summary is for the person deciding whether to isolate fifty machines; the indicators and rules are for the people who will do it. Separate observed facts from your assessments, and say how confident you are.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Tensor parallelism: column and row splits of the MLP and attention
md: Misconception: more TP is a free way to save memory. Per-GPU TP traffic stays near 8bsh per layer however large t gets, every GEMM gets t times smaller (lower GPU efficiency), and once t exceeds the GPUs in one server the all-reduces leave NVLink for the much slower network. Narayanan et al.'s Takeaway 1: use TP up to the server size (8 on DGX A100), then PP across servers.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Size classes: buying speed with internal waste
md: `sizeof` is not what you pay. With a million 130-byte records you might budget 124 MiB, but jemalloc hands out 160 bytes each (153 MiB) and a power-of-two allocator 256 (244 MiB). Measure with `malloc_usable_size` or allocator stats, not by multiplying `sizeof`.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Acquire and release: publishing data across threads
md: Synchronization needs a pair on the same atomic: a Release (or stronger) write and an Acquire (or stronger) read that observes that write or its release sequence. Then everything before the write is visible after the read.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: RCU: publish a new version, free the old after a grace period
md: RCU protects readers from updaters, not updaters from each other. `rcu_assign_pointer()` does not make two concurrent updates safe; the example still takes `foo_mutex`. And a pointer from `rcu_dereference()` is valid only inside the critical section that fetched it.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Heap overflow: corrupting the neighbouring object
md: A heap overflow damages whoever happens to be next, and you cannot predict who that is: it depends on the allocator, the sizes and the order of allocations. Treat any heap overflow as able to corrupt any nearby object.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Triplet loss: the margin and easy, semi-hard, hard negatives
md: Hard is not the same as useful. The very hardest negatives in a large dataset are often mislabeled or badly imaged examples (FaceNet names both). Training only on them teaches the network to fit noise.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Warm caches in the benchmark, cold caches in production
md: A microbenchmark's working set and access pattern are part of the experiment. Report them next to the time, and sweep the size if the code's data can be large.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Token-in-token-out: train on the tokens you actually sampled
md: `role_content_only` is marked high risk. A tool-calling turn often has empty visible text, so two turns that called different tools can match. The stored prefix then wins, and the trainer keeps a history showing a call the agent never made, silently.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Learned indexes: a model that predicts where a key lives
md: Model execution must be nearly free. The paper's first attempt ran a 2-layer, 32-neuron net through TensorFlow from Python: about 80,000 ns per prediction, versus about 300 ns for a whole B-tree traversal. Their Learning Index Framework instead extracts the trained weights and generates small C++ index code, never calling TensorFlow at lookup time.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: MLA in production: kernels, prefill, parallelism, results
md: Do not credit MLA with every DeepSeek-V2 headline. Against DeepSeek 67B, V2 reports a 93.3% smaller KV cache and 5.76x maximum generation throughput (over 50K tokens per second on one node of eight H800s, NVIDIA data-center GPUs), but the deployed system also used FP8 weights, KV cache quantization to about 6 bits per element, and a sparse MoE. The 42.5% training cost saving comes from MoE, not MLA.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Why one phrasing of a question misses relevant documents
md: Retrieval quality depends on the exact words of the query. Multi-query retrieval treats the user's wording as one sample from many possible phrasings and retrieves with several samples instead of betting on one.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Bi-encoder, late interaction, cross-encoder: where the cost goes
md: Precompute versus interact. The more of the query-document comparison happens at query time, the more accurate and the more expensive the scorer. Bi-encoders and late interaction can serve as first stages over an index; cross-encoders only fit on short candidate lists.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Reusing the extra heads to decode faster
md: MTP gives two separate benefits: a training signal that can make the main model better, and heads that can draft tokens for exact, faster greedy decoding. You can use the first without the second by discarding the heads.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Scaling Muon to LLMs, distributing it, and choosing an optimizer
md: Do not judge an optimizer by a single untuned comparison. The Muon post argues that most papers claiming to beat AdamW used undertuned baselines, and proposes competitive benchmarks (like the NanoGPT speedrun record, where anyone can revert to AdamW) as the standard of evidence.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: From a racy flag to a correct spin lock
md: A lock is two things at once: mutual exclusion (one atomic read-modify-write decides a single winner) and visibility (Acquire on lock, Release on unlock, so each unlock happens-before the next lock).

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Why a database keeps old copies of rows
md: MVCC is not the same as no locking. Two transactions that update the *same* row still conflict: the second one waits for the first to commit or roll back. MVCC only stops readers and writers from blocking each other.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Serializable Snapshot Isolation: catching dangerous structures
md: SSI = snapshot isolation plus non-blocking tracking of rw edges. It aborts a transaction in any dangerous structure, so every committed set is serializable; the application's job is to retry on 40001.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Why long context needs sparsity, and why bolt-on sparsity disappoints
md: Theoretical FLOP savings are not speedups. A sparse attention method is only fast if the GPU reads fewer bytes in contiguous chunks during every phase (training, prefill, decode), and it only keeps quality if the model is trained with the sparsity.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: PDQ, learned copy detectors and building a real pipeline
md: Global hashes, PDQ included, do poorly when one image is a **crop** of another; the PDQ document lists deep crops as out of scope. ImageHash's documentation shows how fast aHash degrades with rotation on its test image: 2 bits at 1 degree, 11 at 6 degrees, 21 at 26 degrees. Large borders, overlaid text and memes also defeat them.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: DHCP starvation and rogue DHCP servers
md: Whoever answers DHCP chooses a device's gateway and DNS server, so a rogue DHCP server is an on-path attack on every device it reaches. Only trusted ports may send DHCP server messages.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: Segmentation, zero trust and the Target breach
md: Segmentation limits how far one compromise spreads; zero trust removes network location as a reason to trust anything. Both assume a breach will happen, and both only pay off when someone watches the alerts at the boundaries.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Ports, sockets and NAT
md: NAT is not a firewall. It drops unsolicited inbound packets only as a side effect of having no table entry. Port-forwarding rules, devices that open forwards automatically, IPv6 (often no NAT at all) and connections started from inside all bypass that "protection". Use an actual firewall policy.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: First touch: the thread that writes a page first picks its node
md: malloc chooses addresses, the first write chooses the node. Initialize data in parallel with the same pinned threads and the same partitioning that will later use it.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Wear leveling, TRIM, hot and cold data, endurance
md: Lifetime and throughput both scale with 1/A. The levers to lower A are all about making victim blocks emptier: more spare, TRIM of dead data, writes that are large and sequential, and grouping data that will die at the same time.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Training and tuning a detector in practice
md: The AP number picks the model; the confidence threshold, chosen on validation data that looks like deployment, decides how it behaves.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: What metrics, traces and logs can each answer
md: The shape of the data decides which questions you can ask. Metrics answer "how often, how slow, for everyone". Traces answer "where did the time go inside this one request". Logs answer "what exactly happened at this instant".

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: SLOs, error budgets, burn-rate alerts, and the 03:00 dashboard
md: A dashboard is an ordered list of questions, not a list of metrics. Start with the SLO burn rate (are users hurt), then symptoms (what is broken), then causes and changes (why), then one link into a single trace (prove it).

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Judging answers on documents with ANLS
md: ANLS = average over questions of the best (1 minus normalized edit distance) against any ground truth, zeroed when the distance reaches 0.5. It rewards nearly right reading, not semantic equivalence.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Privilege separation: OpenSSH's design case
md: Privilege separation protects only the code that was moved into the unprivileged half. regreSSHion (CVE-2024-6387, covered in linux-for-security) was a signal-handler race in sshd's privileged code which, in Qualys's words, "is not sandboxed and runs with full privileges". That is why OpenSSH keeps shrinking the privileged parts: the 9.8 and 10.0 splits move more code out of them.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: Targets, PUBLIC vs PRIVATE, and why links fail
md: Choosing PRIVATE for a dependency that appears in your public headers compiles fine for you and breaks for your users: their code includes your header, which includes D's header, but D's include directory never reached them. The error shows up in *their* build as a missing header.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Why flaky tests ruin big suites: the probability
md: Small flake rates multiply across big suites: $P(\text{green}) = (1-p)^{\,N}$. Reruns buy back greens at the cost of hiding intermittent real failures. Fixing the flaky test is the only option without that cost.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Why reviewer response time dominates time to merge
md: Fast does not mean shallow. Google's guide says reviewers must spend enough time that their approval really means the code meets the standard, and that if a change is too large to review quickly, the right response is to ask for it to be split into smaller changes, or at least send early comments on the overall design.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: AI-assisted contributions: label it, keep a human in the loop, or not
md: Common misconception: "I reviewed it, so I do not need to mention the tool." Under LLVM's policy review is required **and** substantial tool use should still be labelled. Under QEMU's policy, reviewing it does not help: AI-generated content is declined. The rules are per project.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Pushing rewritten history: --force-with-lease and its limits
md: The manual's own warning: a bare `--force-with-lease` interacts very badly with anything that runs `git fetch` in the background, such as an IDE (integrated development environment, your code editor) or a cron job. Each background fetch refreshes the expectation, so the lease can no longer tell "I saw this" from "something fetched this".

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: License compatibility: can these two pieces of code be combined?
md: Compatibility is about combining code into one work. Permissive code flows into almost anything; copyleft code only flows into the same copyleft, and version clauses like 'only' and 'or later' decide which.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Noise and bias: making before and after comparable
md: Repetition fights noise; only experimental design fights bias. Same machine, same build flags, interleaved or balanced run order, and a second setup for surprising results.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Find the commit behind a change: log -S, -G and -L
md: Pick the tool by question. Who last touched this line: `git blame -w -M`. When did this text appear or disappear: `git log -S'text'`. Which commits touched lines matching a pattern: `git log -G'regex'`. How did this function evolve: `git log -L :func:file`. Then read the commit message and its pull request.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Intermittent bugs, seeds, and environment differences
md: Do not say "it is random". Tatham's advice is to try it several times, on another machine if you can, and report how often it fails and any pattern you notice, even a probabilistic one.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Self-review the diff, then use drafts to signal readiness
md: Misconception: "I will clean it up after review starts." Reviewers read what is there. Opening a non-draft PR with failing tests, debug code or an empty description tells them it is ready when it is not, and spends their first pass on things you could have caught.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, and when caching pays
md: Longest-prefix-first can starve a request whose prefix is never cached, since others keep jumping ahead. The SGLang paper says so and leaves fair scheduling as future work.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Vulnerability scanners: matching versions to known flaws
md: A clean scan means "the scanner did not find it", not "it is not there". Equifax's scans came back clean twice while a vulnerable, internet-facing application waited to be exploited. Scan results are only as complete as the asset list and the places the scanner can see.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Reading a flame graph: width, top edges and plateaus
md: Look for the widest top edges. Width is share of samples, y is ancestry, x order is alphabetical, and color is decoration.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Transactions: how libpmemobj's undo log survives a crash
md: Undo log: old value durable before new value is written; commit point is invalidating the log. Redo log: new values durable in the log first; commit point is the commit mark. Either way, exactly one 8-byte-atomic event decides old versus new.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Reading headers to triage a suspicious message
md: Do not open links or attachments from a reported message on your own workstation while triaging. Read headers as text, and send URLs and files to a sandbox (lesson 11).

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: What a pose model outputs and the top-down pipeline
md: A pose model's output is a fixed, ordered list of keypoints per person, each with a position and a confidence. Everything downstream (metrics, angles, rep counting) is arithmetic on that list.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Filtering inside the graph walk, and when the graph falls apart
md: Do not read 3% as a safe threshold. Proximity graphs are not random graphs, matching nodes are often clustered, and being connected is weaker than being *navigable*: greedy search can stall in a matching region long before the subgraph formally splits. Qdrant's docs simply warn that the HNSW graph starts to fall apart when filters are too strict.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: After the foothold: the four tactics defenders must see
md: The foothold is rarely the disaster. Escalation, credential theft, discovery and lateral movement turn one infected laptop into a domain-wide incident, and each of them leaves evidence on the machines it touches.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Grading the answer versus grading every step
md: An ORM gets one label per solution and must discover where errors are. A PRM is told where the first error is. That extra information is why PRMs rank solutions better on hard problems, and why they can reject right answers reached by wrong reasoning.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: What a switch really costs: direct work and cold caches
md: Misconception: "a context switch costs a few microseconds, so it does not matter." That is the direct cost on an idle cache. Li et al. found the total ranged from several microseconds to more than a thousand, depending on working set size and access pattern. Benchmarks that touch no data hide the part that hurts.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Why hand-tuned prompts are brittle
md: Prompt optimization is search: candidates (instructions and demos), a metric, a dev set to score on, and a proposer. Everything else in this course is a choice of proposer, a way to spend the budget, or a way to keep the final number honest.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: The funnel: from 100 backbones to a binder that works
md: More sampling buys you less than independence suggests. Sequence sampling cannot rescue an undesignable backbone, which is why designability of the generator, measured at a fixed small M, is the metric the backbone papers compete on.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Hashing files and checking them against known-bad lists
md: A hash match is strong evidence; a hash miss proves nothing. Security researcher David Bianco's [Pyramid of Pain](https://detect-respond.blogspot.com/2013/03/the-pyramid-of-pain.html) puts hash values at the bottom because changing a single byte gives the attacker a brand new hash. Use hash lists to catch known copies quickly, never as the only control.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Synonym expansion on the toy corpus: recall up, precision at risk
md: Misconception: expansion always helps. It helps when the added words mean the same thing **in this query's context**. *auto* means automobile in d6 but automatic in d9; a list that ignores sense trades recall for false matches. Here the bad synonym cost nothing at the top only because the good documents happened to score higher.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Plain binary quantization: one sign bit per dimension
md: Sign bits only carry information if coordinates are spread around zero. Qdrant's docs say binary quantization needs a *centered distribution* of vector components. If every coordinate is positive, every bit is 1 and all vectors look identical; non-negative data such as SIFT (scale-invariant feature transform) image descriptors comes close to this. Lesson 2 measures this failure.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Raft leader election: terms, votes and randomized timeouts
md: `currentTerm`, `votedFor` (the candidate this server voted for in the current term) and the log must reach stable storage *before* a server answers an RPC. If a server voted, crashed, and forgot its vote, it could vote again in the same term for a different candidate, and two leaders could be elected for one term.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Evaluating retrieval and generation separately
md: Read the metrics as a grid. Low context recall: a **retrieval** problem. High context recall but low faithfulness: a **generation** problem. High faithfulness but wrong answer: the context itself was wrong or stale, an **index** problem.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: nDCG precisely: gain, discount, log base and the ideal
md: nDCG has four knobs: the gain (linear or exponential), the discount (modern log2(i+1) or the original base b form), the cutoff k, and where the ideal comes from (all qrels, not the run). Report all four or your number cannot be reproduced.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: InfiniBand, RoCEv2 and iWARP: what carries the packets
md: RoCEv2 gets RDMA onto ordinary routed Ethernet only by making that Ethernet (nearly) lossless with PFC, then taming PFC's side effects with end-to-end congestion control such as DCQCN. Loss is still possible from corruption or misconfiguration, and go-back-N recovery makes it expensive.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Showing other players: interpolation and lag compensation
md: The local player lives in the **present** (prediction); everyone else is shown in the **past** (interpolation); the server reconciles the two when it matters (lag compensation).

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Cold start: content for new items, bandits for new users
md: Cold start is a data problem, so the fixes are other data: content features for new items, context and popularity for new users, then controlled exploration to collect the interactions CF needs.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: When each join wins: row counts, probes and memory
md: `work_mem` is a limit per sort or hash operation, not per query. A plan with three hash joins and a sort can use several multiples of it, and many sessions can do so at once. Raising it globally to fix one query can exhaust memory.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Failures: sloppy quorums, hinted handoff and repair
md: A write that *fails* (fewer than W acks before the timeout) is not rolled back. It may sit on a minority of replicas and later spread through repair or hints. The Cassandra docs warn that without blocking read repair such a write "may be visible in one read, and then disappear in a subsequent read". "Failed" means "outcome unknown", not "did not happen".

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: Catching hacks: CoT monitors, obfuscation, generalization
md: Use the CoT monitor to **detect** problems and fix environments, but avoid strong optimization pressure directly on the CoT. Baker et al. call the cost of keeping CoTs monitorable (for example a slightly less capable or more expensive model) a **monitorability tax**. They also note that even patching only the bugs a monitor finds may put slight pressure toward hacks it cannot see.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Treating risk: accept, mitigate, transfer, avoid
md: "Transfer" moves money, not responsibility. An insurer may pay for forensics and claims, and a contract may make a vendor liable, but regulators and customers still hold you accountable for the breach of your data, and insurers can deny claims when the controls you declared on the application form were not really in place (lesson 17).

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: SOC 2: trust services criteria, Type I vs II, and your evidence
md: SOC 2 is a CPA's opinion on your controls against the Trust Services Criteria. Type I: designed and in place on a date. Type II: operating effectively over a period, tested by sampling. Most of the evidence is ordinary engineering records, if your process creates them.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Third-party risk: questionnaires, SBOMs and concentration risk
md: Tier vendors by access and criticality; use standard questionnaires and independent reports with their scope, exceptions and user-entity controls; write breach notice and exit into contracts; collect SBOMs so a new CVE becomes a query; and record shared dependencies as their own concentration risks with fallbacks.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: The long tail: why one response can idle a whole cluster
md: Partial rollouts are not free. A trajectory stitched from segments generated by several policy versions is off-policy data. Kimi notes some segments can be excluded from the loss; AReaL's interruptible rollouts face the same issue and handle it with a modified PPO objective.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: Placing GEMM, softmax and LLM decode on the roofline
md: Intensity is not fixed for a given operation. It depends on shape (thin GEMMs fall left), precision (FP8 halves the bytes per element and so doubles intensity), and how well the implementation reuses data. A naive GEMM that rereads inputs from DRAM can be memory bound even at 8192 cubed.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Why fuse ranks instead of scores
md: An RRF score is not a relevance probability. Its size depends on k and on how many lists were fused (Azure AI Search notes each query contributes at most about $1/k$), so do not apply a fixed threshold to it across queries or configurations.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Bindings, helpers, abstractions: the layers under a Rust driver
md: Misconception: "Rust drivers do not need cleanup code." They need exactly as much cleanup as C drivers. The difference is that it lives once in a `Drop` impl (yours or an abstraction's) and runs on every path automatically, including early returns from `?`.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: The scheduling cycle: select_cpu, enqueue, dispatch, run
md: Where a task finally runs is decided when it lands in a local DSQ, usually inside `ops.dispatch()` on the CPU that is asking for work. `select_cpu` is an optimization: matching the final CPU saves a bit of work, and picking an idle CPU wakes it up.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Biba and integrity: no read down, no write up
md: Confidentiality: no read up, no write down. Integrity: no read down, no write up. If you remember which way information is allowed to flow, you can rebuild both rule sets.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Identity-aware proxies and ZTNA versus the VPN
md: A proxy only protects an application if it is the only way in and the application can tell the difference. Signed, audience-bound assertions let the application check for itself.
